title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XIII: The Song of Sigemund (lines 837–924)
part: Fitt XIII · The Song of Sigemund (lines 837–924)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 32–35, lines 837–924 (fitt XIII). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Ðā wæs on morgen mīne gefrǣge
ymb þā gifhealle gūðrinc monig;
sentences.l: Then was in the morning, by my hearing, about the gift-hall, many a war-man;
sentences.i: Then, as I have heard, in the morning there were many warriors about the gift-hall;
sentences.n: This unit opens the fitt; the sentence before it ended in the last part, and ‘Ðā’ here is ‘then’. ‘Ðā wæs … gūðrinc monig’ is ‘then was … many a war-man’: ‘gūðrinc’ is singular but ‘monig’ makes it mean many men, so the verb is singular too. ‘on morgen’ is ‘in the morning’ (the next day after the night’s fighting, as the lines that follow show). ‘mīne gefrǣge’ is ‘by my hearing’, a stock phrase for ‘as I have heard’: the poet steps in as reporter and tells us he is relaying what he was told. ‘ymb þā gifhealle’ is ‘about the gift-hall’, ‘gifhealle’ being ‘giefu’, ‘gift’, and ‘heall’, ‘hall’, the hall where the king gives out rings, which is Heorot.

sentences.t:
fērdon folctogan feorran ond neân
geond wīdwegas wundor scēawian,
lāþes lāstas.
sentences.l: Went folk-leaders from far and from near along wide-ways, the wonder to look at, the hated-one’s tracks.
sentences.i: From far and from near the leaders of the people went along the broad roads to look at the marvel, the tracks of the hated one.
sentences.n: ‘fērdon’ is the past plural of ‘fēran’, ‘go, travel’, with ‘folctogan’ (‘folc’, ‘people’, and ‘toga’, ‘leader’) as its plural subject; the verb stands first. ‘feorran’ is ‘from far’ and ‘neân’ is ‘from near’; the circumflex in ‘neân’ is Klaeber’s mark for a contracted vowel, which our text sets on the second letter of the pair. ‘geond wīdwegas’ is ‘along wide-ways’, wide roads. ‘scēawian’ is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to look at’ (‘show’ and ‘sheen’ are its cousins), and ‘wundor’ is its object, ‘a wonder’. ‘lāþes lāstas’ is in apposition to it: ‘lāð’ is ‘hateful’, and ‘lāþes’ is a genitive used as a noun, ‘of the hated one’, with ‘lāstas’, ‘tracks, footprints’. The hated one is the monster who fled from the hall.

sentences.t:
Nō his līfgedāl
sārlīc þūhte secga ǣnẹgum
þāra þe tīrlēases trode scēawode,
sentences.l: Not his life-parting grievous seemed to any of men, of those who the glory-less-one’s track looked at,
sentences.i: His parting from life seemed grievous to none of the men, to none of those who looked upon the track of the glory-less one,
sentences.n: ‘Nō … ǣnẹgum’ is ‘not … to any’: the negative ‘nō’ at the head of the clause negates it, so ‘any’ comes to mean ‘none’. ‘his līfgedāl’ is the subject, ‘life-parting’, death. ‘sārlīc’ is ‘sore’, grievous, and ‘þūhte’ is the past of ‘þyncan’, ‘seem’, with the dative ‘secga ǣnẹgum’, ‘to any of men’. The dot under the ‘e’ of ‘ǣnẹgum’ is Klaeber’s sign that this vowel does not count in the metre, so the word is scanned as if the vowel were not there; it is a mark for the reader of the verse and changes nothing in the sense. ‘þāra þe’ is ‘of those who’, and ‘scēawode’ is singular because each man is thought of in turn. ‘tīrlēases’ is ‘tīr’, ‘glory’, and ‘lēas’, ‘without’, the glory-less one, a genitive singular; ‘trode’ I take as the object of ‘scēawode’, the ‘track’ he left, though its ending is not the plain accusative, so that is read from the sense. The men do not grieve at his death.

sentences.t:
hū hē wērigmōd on weg þanon,
nīða ofercumen, on nicera mere
fǣge ond geflȳmed feorhlāstas bær.
sentences.l: how he, weary-minded, away from there, of strifes overcome, to the nickers’ mere, doomed and put-to-flight, life-tracks bore.
sentences.i: how, weary in spirit, overcome in the struggles, doomed and put to flight, he carried the tracks of his life away from there to the mere of the water-monsters.
sentences.n: ‘hū’ opens an indirect question after ‘scēawode’: what they saw was how he went. ‘wērigmōd’ is ‘wērig’, ‘weary’, and ‘mōd’, ‘mind’, and ‘on weg þanon’ is ‘away from there’. ‘nīða ofercumen’ is ‘nīða’, genitive plural of ‘nīð’, ‘strife’, and ‘ofercumen’, ‘overcome’; the genitive after it is read as ‘in the struggles’; Klaeber’s apparatus lists other readings (‘oferwunnen’, ‘genǣged’) offered by editors, so the phrase is not secure. ‘nicera’ is the genitive plural of ‘nicor’, ‘water-monster’, so the mere is the ‘nickers’ mere’. ‘fǣge’ is ‘doomed to die’ and ‘geflȳmed’ is ‘put to flight’, both agreeing with ‘hē’. ‘feorhlāstas bær’ is ‘bore life-tracks’; the compound is not found elsewhere, and my sense, that his flight left the traces of his life (his blood) on the way, is a guess. Some editors print ‘feorlāstas’, ‘far-tracks’, which Klaeber lists but does not take.

sentences.l: There was in blood the surf welling, the terrible wave-swing all mingled, with hot gore, with sword-blood it welled;
sentences.i: There the surf was boiling with blood, the dreadful surge of the waves all mixed with it, and welled up with hot gore, with the blood of the sword;
sentences.n: ‘Ðǣr’ is ‘there’, at the mere. ‘brim weallende’ is ‘surf welling’, ‘weallende’ being a present participle after ‘wæs’; ‘brim’ is the sea or surf, and ‘on blōde’ is ‘in blood’. ‘atol ȳða geswing’ is ‘terrible wave-swing’: ‘ȳða’ is genitive plural of ‘ȳð’, ‘wave’, and ‘geswing’ is a surging or turmoil. ‘eal gemenged’ is ‘all mingled’, a participle. ‘hāton heolfre’ is ‘with hot gore’: ‘hāton’ is the adjective ‘hāt’, ‘hot’, agreeing with ‘heolfre’ in the dative singular, but its ending is odd: a strong dative would be ‘hātum’ and a weak one ‘hātan’, so I take ‘-on’ as a spelling of one of those (it is not the verb ‘hātan’, ‘call’), and ‘heolfre’ is ‘gore’. ‘heorodrēore’ is ‘heoru’, ‘sword’, and ‘drēor’, ‘gore’, so ‘sword-gore’, battle-blood. ‘wēol’ is the past of ‘weallan’, ‘well, boil’.

sentences.t: dēaðfǣge dēof;
sentences.l: death-doomed, he dived;
sentences.i: doomed to die, he plunged;
sentences.n: The verb in this unit is a guess. ‘dēaðfǣge’ is ‘dēaþ’, ‘death’, and ‘fǣge’, ‘doomed’; its ‘-e’ is the ordinary nominative singular masculine ending of ‘fǣge’ (the same form as ‘fǣge’ at 846), agreeing with an understood ‘he’. The last word is the hard one. The manuscript has ‘deog’, and Klaeber’s italic ‘f’ in ‘dēof’ is his sign that he changed the manuscript’s letter there. The apparatus lists the other attempts: ‘dēag’ (‘the dye’, as if the water was dyed), ‘dēog’ (‘dyed’, or ‘hid himself’), ‘dēop’ (‘deep’), and ‘dēaf’, which a number of editors accept and which Klaeber’s ‘dēof’ is said to equal. ‘dēaf’ is the past of ‘dūfan’, ‘dive, sink’, and with ‘siððan’ and the laying down of life in the next lines it makes the best sense, so I give ‘dived’; the verb ‘to dive’ comes from it.

sentences.t:
siððan drēama lēas
in fenfreoðo feorh ālegde,
hǣþene sāwle; þǣr him hel onfēng.
sentences.l: after, of-joys bereft, in the fen-refuge his life he laid down, the heathen soul; there him hell received.
sentences.i: when, bereft of joys, he laid down his life in his refuge in the fen, that heathen soul; there hell took him in.
sentences.n: ‘siððan’ is ‘after’ or ‘when’. ‘drēama lēas’ is ‘without joys’: ‘lēas’ takes a genitive, and ‘drēama’ is the genitive plural of ‘drēam’, ‘joy’. ‘fenfreoðo’ is ‘fen-refuge’, ‘fen’ and ‘freoðo’, ‘protection, shelter’, the monster’s den in the marsh, with ‘in’ and the accusative of the place he went to die. ‘feorh ālegde’ is ‘laid down life’, the past of ‘ālecgan’, ‘lay down, give up’, and ‘hǣþene sāwle’ is ‘heathen soul’ in apposition to ‘feorh’, accusative singular feminine. ‘þǣr him hel onfēng’ is ‘there hell received him’: ‘onfēng’ is the past of ‘onfōn’, ‘receive’, ‘hel’ is a feminine noun, the underworld, and ‘him’ is dative. The poet, a Christian, says the creature went to hell.

sentences.t:
Þanon eft gewiton ealdgesīðas
swylce geong manig of gomenwāþe,
fram mere mōdge mēarum rīdan,
beornas on blancum.
sentences.l: From there back departed old-companions, likewise young many from the joy-going, from the mere high-spirited on horses to ride, men on white-horses.
sentences.i: From there the old companions rode back, and many young men too, in high spirits, from the merry going out, away from the mere on their horses, men on their white steeds.
sentences.n: ‘Þanon eft gewiton’ is ‘from there back departed’; ‘gewiton’ is the past plural of ‘gewītan’, ‘go’. ‘ealdgesīðas’ is ‘eald’, ‘old’, and ‘gesīð’, ‘companion’, the veterans of the troop, and ‘swylce geong manig’ is ‘likewise many a young one’; the sense of ‘ealdgesīðas’ is from its parts, since the word is rare. ‘gomenwāþe’ is a compound, ‘gomen’, ‘mirth, play’, and ‘wāþ’, ‘going, wandering’; I take ‘of gomenwāþe’ as ‘from the merry going’, the outing, a guess from the pieces. ‘mōdge’ is nominative plural, ‘high-spirited’, and ‘mēarum rīdan’ is ‘to ride on horses’ (‘mēarum’ is a dative plural of ‘mearh’, ‘horse’), an infinitive of manner after ‘gewiton’. ‘blancum’ is the dative plural of ‘blanca’, ‘white horse’ (the word is the ancestor of ‘blank’), and ‘beornas’ is ‘men, warriors’ in apposition.

sentences.t:
Ðǣr wæs Bēowulfes
mǣrðo mǣned;
sentences.l: There was Beowulf’s glory told of;
sentences.i: There Beowulf’s glory was spoken of;
sentences.n: ‘Ðǣr’ is ‘there’, among the riders. ‘Bēowulfes mǣrðo’ is ‘Beowulf’s glory’, ‘mǣrðo’ being a form of ‘mǣrðu’, ‘fame, glorious deed’, here the subject; it may be read as a singular feminine collective (so the verb ‘wæs’ is singular) or as a plural with the singular verb. ‘mǣned’ is the participle of ‘mǣnan’, ‘tell of, mention’. The riders praise him as they go.

sentences.t:
monig oft gecwæð,
þætte sūð nē norð be sǣm twēonum
ofer eormengrund ōþer nǣnig
under swegles begong sēlra nǣre
rondhæbbendra, rīces wyrðra. —
sentences.l: many often said, that south nor north between the seas two over the earth-ground another none under the sky’s circuit better were-not of shield-bearers, of rule worthier. —
sentences.i: many a man said again and again that no other among shield-bearers, south or north between the two seas, over all the wide earth under the sky’s round, was better or more worthy of rule. —
sentences.n: ‘monig oft gecwæð’ is ‘many often said’, ‘gecwæð’ being the past of ‘gecweðan’, ‘say’. ‘þætte’ is ‘þæt ðe’, ‘that’, and opens what they said; the verb inside it is subjunctive, so ‘nǣre’ is ‘ne wǣre’, ‘were not’ in reported speech. ‘sūð nē norð’ is ‘south nor north’, and ‘be sǣm twēonum’ is ‘between the seas two’, ‘between the two seas’. Which two seas are meant is not said; the phrase just means that nowhere in the world is there his equal. ‘ofer eormengrund’ is ‘over the earth-ground’, ‘eormen’ meaning ‘huge’ and ‘grund’ ‘ground’; ‘under swegles begong’ is ‘under the sky’s circuit’, ‘begong’ being a compass or realm. ‘ōþer nǣnig … sēlra’ is ‘another none … better’, with ‘rondhæbbendra’, ‘of shield-bearers’, in the genitive plural after it, and ‘rīces wyrðra’ is ‘worthier of rule’, ‘wyrðra’ being the comparative of ‘wyrðe’, ‘worthy’, with the genitive. The dash opens an aside.

sentences.t:
Nē hīe hūru winedrihten wiht ne lōgon,
glædne Hrōðgār, ac þæt wæs gōd cyning. —
sentences.l: Not they indeed the friend-lord a whit blamed, the glad Hrothgar, but that was a good king. —
sentences.i: Not that they found any fault with their friend and lord, gracious Hrothgar; no, he was a good king. —
sentences.n: This is the aside the dashes close. ‘Nē hīe hūru … wiht ne lōgon’ is ‘not they indeed … at all blamed’: ‘lōgon’ is the past plural of ‘lēan’, ‘blame’, and the second negative, ‘wiht ne’, ‘not a whit’, strengthens the first, as Old English does. ‘winedrihten’ is ‘wine’, ‘friend’, and ‘dryhten’, ‘lord’, the friend-lord, and ‘glædne Hrōðgār’ is an accusative in apposition, ‘glad Hrothgar’, ‘glæd’ meaning ‘bright, gracious’. ‘ac þæt wæs gōd cyning’ is ‘but that was a good king’. The poet breaks off to say that praising the guest above all other shield-bearers is no slur on his host.

sentences.t:
Hwīlum heaþorōfe hlēapan lēton,
on geflit faran fealwe mēaras,
ðǣr him foldwegas fægere þūhton,
cystum cūðe.
sentences.l: At whiles, battle-bold ones let leap, to go into a contest, fallow horses, where to them the earth-ways fair seemed, in excellences known.
sentences.i: Sometimes the battle-bold riders let their dun horses leap and race one another, where the ground seemed fair to them, horses famed for their excellence.
sentences.n: ‘Hwīlum’ is ‘at whiles’, ‘sometimes’, the dative plural of ‘hwīl’ used as an adverb (the same as at 175 in the second part). ‘heaþorōfe’ is ‘heaþu’, ‘battle’, and ‘rōf’, ‘bold’, nominative plural, the riders, who are the subject of ‘lēton’, ‘let’, with the infinitives ‘hlēapan’, ‘leap’, and ‘faran’, ‘go’. The object is ‘fealwe mēaras’, ‘fallow (dun) horses’, accusative plural. ‘on geflit’ is ‘into a contest’, a race. ‘ðǣr him foldwegas fægere þūhton’ is ‘where to them the earth-ways seemed fair’, ‘foldweg’ being ‘folde’, ‘earth’, and ‘weg’, ‘way’, and ‘þūhton’ a past of ‘þyncan’. ‘cystum cūðe’ is ‘known for excellences’, ‘cystum’ a dative plural of ‘cyst’, ‘choice, excellence’; the plural ‘cūðe’ could agree with the horses, with the riders, or even with ‘foldwegas’ (the ground ‘known for its excellences’), and I take it with the horses.

sentences.t:
Hwīlum cyninges þegn,
guma gilphlæden, gidda gemyndig,
sē ðe ealfela ealdgesegena
worn gemunde — word ōþer fand
sōðe gebunden — secg eft ongan
sīð Bēowulfes snyttrum styrian,
sentences.l: At whiles a king’s thane, a man laden-with-praise, of songs mindful, he who all-many of old-sayings a store remembered — word other found truly bound — the man again began Beowulf’s journey with skill to stir,
sentences.i: At other times a king’s thane, a man laden with praise and mindful of lays, who remembered a great store of old tales — he found one word truly bound to another — in his turn began to take up Beowulf’s exploit and set it going with skill,
sentences.n: The second ‘Hwīlum’ sets a second pastime beside the racing. The subject is ‘cyninges þegn’, ‘a king’s thane’, with ‘guma gilphlæden’ in apposition: ‘gilp’ is ‘boast, praise’ and ‘hlæden’ is the participle of ‘hladan’, ‘load’, so ‘laden with praise’, the poet of the court. ‘gidda gemyndig’ is ‘mindful of songs’, since ‘gemyndig’ takes a genitive, ‘gidda’ the genitive plural of ‘gidd’, ‘song, lay’. ‘sē ðe … worn gemunde’ is ‘he who remembered a store’ of ‘ealfela ealdgesegena’, ‘very many old sayings’. The dashes enclose ‘word ōþer fand sōðe gebunden’, literally ‘word other found truly bound’; ‘word’ is singular, so it is most likely ‘he found another word, truly bound’ (to the one before); ‘gebunden’ may mean linked by alliteration in the verse, but that is a guess. ‘secg eft ongan’ is ‘the man again began’, and ‘eft’ may be ‘in turn’. ‘sīð Bēowulfes snyttrum styrian’ is ‘to stir Beowulf’s journey with skill’: ‘sīð’ is his adventure, ‘snyttrum’ the dative plural of ‘snytru’, ‘wisdom, skill’, and ‘styrian’, ‘stir, set in motion’, here ‘to take up’.

sentences.t:
ond on spēd wrecan spel gerāde,
wordum wrixlan;
sentences.l: and with success to utter a tale rightly, with words to vary;
sentences.i: and to tell a fitting tale with ease, ringing changes on his words;
sentences.n: The infinitives ‘wrecan’ and ‘wrixlan’ still depend on ‘ongan’. ‘on spēd’ is ‘with success’, ‘spēd’ meaning ‘prosperity, speed, ability’, so he tells it readily. ‘wrecan’ is ‘drive out, utter’ (the ancestor of ‘wreak’), and ‘spel’ is ‘tale’, its object. ‘gerāde’ is a hard word: I take it as an adjective or adverb meaning ‘apt, aptly’, but the form is uncertain and the sense is a guess from the context. ‘wordum wrixlan’ is ‘to change with words’, to vary or interchange the words, which fits a singer who works the same story into new phrasing.

sentences.t:
wēlhwylc gecwæð,
þæt hē fram Sigemunde[s] secgan hȳrde
ellendǣdum, uncūþes fela,
Wælsinges gewin, wīde sīðas,
sentences.l: every-one he said, that he of Sigemund’s valor-deeds to say heard, much unknown, the Wælsing’s strife, wide journeys,
sentences.i: he told everything, all that he had heard said of Sigemund’s feats of valor, many strange things, the Wælsing’s struggles, his far journeys,
sentences.n: The first clause is hard. ‘wēlhwylc gecwæð’ I take as ‘he said every one’, ‘wēlhwylc’ being the object, an indefinite ‘every one’, and ‘þæt hē … hȳrde’ ‘that he had heard’ spelling out what; but ‘wēlhwylc’ could also be a subject, ‘each said’, so the reading is not certain. ‘fram Sigemunde[s] … ellendǣdum’ is ‘about Sigemund’s valorous deeds’. The manuscript has ‘sige munde’, and Klaeber adds the genitive ending in square brackets, as Grein, Schücking and Sedgefield do (Holthausen would write ‘Sigmundes’), because with the added ‘s’ the name stands in the genitive with ‘ellendǣdum’, the dative plural of ‘ellendǣd’, ‘deed of courage’. ‘secgan hȳrde’ is ‘heard tell’. Sigemund is the hero of an old tale of which a part is told here; the lines say that he was a famous adventurer and that his nephew was his comrade. ‘uncūþes fela’ is ‘much of the unknown’, ‘uncūþes’ the genitive of ‘uncūþ’, ‘unknown, strange’. ‘Wælsinges gewin’ is ‘the Wælsing’s strife’: a ‘Wælsing’ is a son of Wæls, as the story says again at 897, and ‘gewin’ is ‘struggle’. ‘wīde sīðas’ is accusative plural, ‘wide journeys’.

sentences.t:
þāra þe gumena bearn gearwe ne wiston,
fǣhðe ond fyrena,
sentences.l: of those things that the children of men clearly not knew, of feud and of crimes,
sentences.i: such as the children of men had no good knowledge of, of feud and of wickedness,
sentences.n: ‘þāra þe’ is ‘of those which’ and goes back to ‘uncūþes fela’: the tale holds things men had not known before. ‘gumena bearn’ is ‘children of men’, with ‘bearn’ the nominative plural, and ‘wiston’ is the past plural of ‘witan’, ‘know’, with ‘ne’ before it; ‘gearwe’ is ‘clearly, well’. ‘fǣhðe ond fyrena’ are genitives, ‘of feud and of crimes’: ‘fǣhðe’ is ‘fǣhðu’, ‘hostility, feud’ (the ancestor of ‘feud’), and ‘fyrena’ the genitive plural of ‘fyren’, ‘crime, sin’. They say what those unknown things were about.

sentences.t:
būton Fitela mid hine,
þonne hē swulces hwæt secgan wolde,
ēam his nefan,
sentences.l: except Fitela with him, when he of such something to say wished, the uncle to his nephew,
sentences.i: except Fitela, who was with him, whenever he, the uncle, wished to tell his nephew something of the kind,
sentences.n: ‘būton Fitela mid hine’ is ‘except Fitela with him’; ‘mid’ here takes the accusative ‘hine’, which happens beside the dative. Fitela is Sigemund’s nephew, as the line says, and the only one who shared what Sigemund had to say. ‘þonne hē swulces hwæt secgan wolde’ is ‘when he wished to say something of such’: ‘swulces’ is ‘swylces’, genitive singular of ‘swylc’, ‘such’, and ‘hwæt’ is ‘something’, so ‘something of the kind’. ‘ēam his nefan’ is ‘uncle to his nephew’; ‘ēam’ is nominative singular, in apposition to ‘hē’, and ‘nefan’ is dative singular (the form ‘nefan’ is also the nominative plural, but ‘ēam’ is not a plural form). The sense is that Fitela alone had been told these things.

sentences.t:
swā hīe ā wǣron
æt nīða gehwām nȳdgesteallan;
sentences.l: as they ever were at every one of strifes need-comrades;
sentences.i: for they were always comrades in need in every fight;
sentences.n: ‘swā’ is ‘as, since’. ‘hīe ā wǣron’ is ‘they were always’, ‘ā’ being ‘ever’. ‘æt nīða gehwām’ is ‘at each of strifes’, ‘nīða’ a genitive plural and ‘gehwām’ a dative singular, ‘each’, so ‘in every fight’. ‘nȳdgesteallan’ is ‘nȳd’, ‘need, bond’, and ‘gestealla’, ‘comrade’ (the ‘stall’ is the place stood in, so a stand-fellow): comrades of necessity, who stand by one another in every need. It is a plural nominative, the predicate after ‘wǣron’, describing ‘hīe’.

sentences.t:
hæfdon ealfela eotena cynnes
sweordum gesǣged.
sentences.l: They had all-many of giants’ kin with swords laid-low.
sentences.i: They had laid very many of the race of giants low with their swords.
sentences.n: ‘hæfdon … gesǣged’ is a pluperfect, ‘had … laid low’, from ‘habban’ and the participle of ‘gesǣgan’, ‘cause to sink, fell’; the verb is rare and the sense is from the context. The subject is the pair, Sigemund and Fitela. ‘ealfela’ is ‘eal’, ‘all’, and ‘fela’, ‘many’, so ‘very many’, with the genitive ‘eotena cynnes’, ‘of the kin of giants’. ‘eotena’ is the genitive plural of ‘eoten’, ‘giant’, written with a small letter; 902 has ‘Ēotenum’ with a capital, and I treat the two words in the note there. ‘sweordum’ is ‘with swords’, a dative plural.

sentences.t:
Sigemunde gesprong
æfter dēaðdæge dōm unlȳtel,
sentences.l: To Sigemund there sprang after death-day judgment not-little,
sentences.i: To Sigemund after his death-day there sprang up no little renown,
sentences.n: ‘Sigemunde gesprong … dōm’ is ‘to Sigemund sprang … fame’: ‘gesprong’ is the past of ‘gespringan’, ‘spring up, arise’, and ‘Sigemunde’ is dative. ‘dōm’ means ‘judgment’, and so ‘repute, glory’; ‘unlȳtel’ is ‘un-’ and ‘lȳtel’, ‘little’, a negative that means ‘great’. The name is written ‘Sigemunde’ here and at 875; Holthausen would print ‘Sigmunde’ in both. ‘æfter dēaðdæge’ is ‘after death-day’, after his death; the poet says the fame arose after the man was dead.

sentences.t:
syþðan wīges heard wyrm ācwealde,
hordes hyrde;
sentences.l: after, hard in battle, a worm he killed, the hoard’s keeper;
sentences.i: after, hard in battle, he killed a serpent, the keeper of a hoard;
sentences.n: ‘syþðan’ is ‘after’, and the clause says how the fame began. ‘wīges heard’ is ‘hard of battle’, ‘wīges’ a genitive of respect, and ‘heard’ is the subject, an adjective standing as a noun (‘the one hard in battle’), so English supplies ‘he’. ‘wyrm’ is the accusative, the old word for ‘serpent, dragon’ (the ‘worm’ of the later tales), and ‘ācwealde’ is the past of ‘ācwellan’, ‘kill’. ‘hordes hyrde’ is ‘the hoard’s keeper’, in apposition, ‘hyrde’ being ‘herdsman, guard’ (as in ‘shepherd’); the guard is the serpent. ‘wyrm’ is ‘worm’ in the literal line and ‘serpent’ in the idiomatic one, here and below.

sentences.t:
hē under hārne stān,
æþelinges bearn āna genēðde
frēcne dǣde,
sentences.l: he under the grey stone, the atheling’s child, alone ventured a perilous deed,
sentences.i: he, the atheling’s son, went alone under the grey stone and ventured the perilous deed,
sentences.n: ‘hē’ is Sigemund, ‘æþelinges bearn’ ‘the atheling’s child’, an apposition: ‘æþeling’ is a prince of the royal house, and the one meant is Wæls, as 897 shows. ‘under hārne stān’ is ‘under the grey stone’, ‘hārne’ accusative singular masculine, so the stone is something he went under, perhaps the rock over the dragon’s lair (the text says no more). ‘āna’ is ‘alone’, and ‘genēðde’ is the past of ‘genēðan’, ‘venture, dare’, with ‘frēcne dǣde’ the thing he dared. I give ‘a perilous deed’, taking ‘dǣde’ as an accusative singular, but the form is not that noun’s plain accusative (‘dǣd’): the same letters are a dative singular, which would make ‘frēcne’ an adverb (‘daringly, in deed’), or an accusative plural (‘perilous deeds’). The case is uncertain and the sense changes little.

sentences.t: ne wæs him Fitela mid;
sentences.l: not was him Fitela with;
sentences.i: Fitela was not with him;
sentences.n: ‘ne wæs him Fitela mid’ is ‘not was him Fitela with’: ‘him’ is the dative governed by ‘mid’, which has been moved to the end of the clause, after ‘Fitela’. So the uncle went alone, without his nephew, and the poet had said that the two were always together in battle: this is the exception.

sentences.t:
hwæþre him gesǣlde, ðæt þæt swurd þurhwōd
wrǣtlīcne wyrm,
sentences.l: yet it happened to him, that that sword passed through the wondrous worm,
sentences.i: yet it was granted him that the sword went right through the wondrous serpent,
sentences.n: ‘hwæþre’ is ‘yet’. ‘him gesǣlde’ is ‘it befell him’, ‘it was granted’, the past of an impersonal ‘gesǣlan’; ‘ðæt’ is the conjunction and ‘þæt swurd’ the subject, ‘that sword’, so ‘ðæt þæt’ is ‘that the’. ‘þurhwōd’ is the past of ‘þurhwadan’, ‘pass through’ (a cousin of ‘wade’). ‘wrǣtlīcne’ is accusative singular masculine of ‘wrǣtlīc’, ‘wondrous, curious’, from ‘wrǣt’, ‘ornament, artful work’; the serpent is marvelous to behold.

sentences.t:
þæt hit on wealle ætstōd,
dryhtlīc īren;
sentences.l: so that it in the wall stood fast, the lordly iron;
sentences.i: so that it stuck fast in the wall, that noble iron;
sentences.n: ‘þæt hit on wealle ætstōd’ is ‘that it stood fast in the wall’: ‘ætstōd’ is the past of ‘ætstandan’, ‘stand fast, stay’, ‘hit’ is the sword, and ‘wealle’ is a dative. The sword went clean through the creature and stuck in the wall behind it (the text says only ‘wall’). ‘dryhtlīc īren’ is ‘lordly iron’, in apposition to ‘hit’: ‘dryhtlīc’ is ‘fit for a lord’, noble, and ‘īren’ is ‘iron’ used for ‘sword’, as elsewhere.

sentences.t: draca morðre swealt.
sentences.l: the dragon by-slaughter died.
sentences.i: the dragon died a violent death.
sentences.n: ‘draca’ is the nominative, ‘dragon’, the Latin word taken into English; in what comes before it is ‘wyrm’, the native word, and the two name the same creature. ‘morðre’ is a dative singular of ‘morðor’, ‘murder, violent death’, here used as an instrument, ‘by slaughter’. ‘swealt’ is the past of ‘sweltan’, ‘die’ (the ancestor of ‘swelter’).

sentences.l: Had the awesome-one by valor won, that he of the ring-hoard enjoy might, at his own judgment;
sentences.i: The fearsome one had won by his courage that he might enjoy the ring-hoard at his own pleasure;
sentences.n: ‘Hæfde … gegongen’ is a pluperfect, ‘had won’, the participle of ‘gegangan’, ‘get by going, achieve’, and ‘elne’ is a dative singular, ‘by courage’. The subject is ‘āglǣca’, the word used of Grendel and of the other monsters in the earlier parts, which I render ‘awesome one’. Here it is the hero, so the word cannot mean only ‘monster’; its first element is disputed, and I keep one rendering for it. ‘þæt hē … brūcan mōste’ is ‘that he might enjoy’, ‘brūcan’ taking the genitive ‘bēahhordes’, ‘of the ring-hoard’, from ‘bēag’, ‘ring’, and ‘hord’, and ‘mōste’ being the past of ‘mōtan’, ‘be allowed’. ‘selfes dōme’ is ‘at his own judgment’, as he himself chose; ‘selfes’ is a genitive and ‘dōme’ a dative.

sentences.l: the sea-boat he loaded, bore into the ship’s bosom bright treasures, Wæls’s offspring;
sentences.i: he loaded the sea-boat and bore the bright treasures into the lap of the ship, Wæls’s son;
sentences.n: ‘sǣbāt gehleōd’ is ‘sea-boat loaded’, ‘sǣ’ and ‘bāt’, ‘boat’; ‘gehleōd’ is the past of ‘gehladan’, ‘load’, and I take it as printed in the manuscript, though most editors correct it to the regular ‘gehlōd’, as the apparatus says. ‘bær on bearm scipes’ is ‘bore into the ship’s bosom’, ‘bearm’ being ‘lap’, so the hold, and ‘beorhte frætwa’ is ‘bright treasures’, accusative plural. ‘Wælses eafera’ is ‘Wæls’s offspring’: ‘eafera’ is ‘son, heir’, and Wæls, the father of the ‘Wælsing’ of 877, is the ‘æþeling’ of 888. So it is Sigemund who loads the ship.

sentences.t: wyrm hāt gemealt.
sentences.l: the worm hot melted.
sentences.i: the serpent melted in the heat.
sentences.n: ‘wyrm hāt gemealt’ is ‘the worm hot melted’: ‘gemealt’ is the past of ‘gemeltan’, ‘melt’, and ‘hāt’ is ‘hot’, which either agrees with ‘wyrm’ or serves as an adverb. The sense, that the creature melted in its own heat, is a reading of the words, not of any statement in them; some editors print ‘hāte’, ‘with heat’. It may refer to the poison and fire of the dragon, or to the heat of the hoard; the text does not say.

sentences.t:
Sē wæs wreccena wīde mǣrost
ofer werþēode, wīgendra hlēo
ellendǣdum — hē þæs ǣr onðāh —,
sentences.l: He was of exiles widely most-famed over the man-nation, of warriors the shelter, in valor-deeds — he before that had thriven —,
sentences.i: He was the most widely famed of wanderers among mankind, the protector of warriors, for his valorous deeds — he had flourished before that —,
sentences.n: ‘Sē’ is ‘that one’, Sigemund. ‘wreccena’ is the genitive plural of ‘wrecca’, ‘exile, wanderer’ (the word is the ancestor of ‘wretch’), so ‘of exiles’, partitive after ‘mǣrost’, the superlative, ‘most famed’; ‘wīde’ is ‘widely’. ‘ofer werþēode’ is ‘over the man-nation’, ‘wer’, ‘man’, and ‘þēod’, ‘people’, so the world of men. ‘wīgendra hlēo’ is ‘shelter of warriors’, as Beowulf addresses Hrothgar at 429; ‘ellendǣdum’ is a dative plural of respect. The aside ‘hē þæs ǣr onðāh’ is hard: ‘onðāh’ I take as the past of ‘onþēon’, ‘thrive’, and ‘þæs ǣr’ as ‘before that’, ‘earlier than the time of Heremōd’s fall’, so ‘he had prospered before that’; this is a guess. The apparatus lists other readings: ‘āron ðāh’ (Cosijn, Holthausen), and ‘ār onþāh’, ‘received honor’.

sentences.t:
siððan Heremōdes hild sweðrode,
eafoð ond ellen.
sentences.l: after Heremod’s battle dwindled, strength and valor.
sentences.i: after Heremod’s fighting-power faded, his strength and his valor.
sentences.n: ‘siððan’ may be ‘after’ or ‘since’, and which it is depends on how ‘onðāh’ in the line before is read. ‘Heremōdes hild sweðrode’ is ‘Heremod’s battle (war-strength) dwindled’: ‘hild’ is ‘battle’, here his fighting power, and ‘sweðrode’ is the past of ‘sweðrian’, ‘die away, grow weak’. Heremōd is a king of the Danes, whom the poet sets beside Sigemund as one who began well and went bad, as the next lines show. ‘eafoð ond ellen’ are two nominatives, ‘strength and valor’, the same pair as at 601 in the ninth part. Klaeber’s italic ‘a’ in ‘eafoð’ marks his change: the manuscript has ‘earfoð’, ‘hardship’, and the editors who followed Grimm read ‘eafoð’, ‘strength’, which fits better with ‘ellen’ and ‘hild’, so he prints that.

sentences.t:
Hē mid Ēotenum wearð
on fēonda geweald forð forlācen,
snūde forsended.
sentences.l: He among Eotens was into foes’ power forth betrayed, swiftly sent away.
sentences.i: Among the Eotens he was given up into the power of his foes, and swiftly sent away.
sentences.n: ‘Hē’ is Heremōd. ‘wearð … forlācen’ is a passive, ‘was … forlācen’, with ‘wearð’ the past of ‘weorþan’, ‘become’. ‘forlācen’ is a guess: it is a participle of a verb I cannot place in the lexica, perhaps ‘for-’ (a prefix of ruin) and ‘lācan’, ‘play, move’, so ‘played away’, handed over by treachery; I give ‘betrayed’ in the literal and ‘given up’ in the other. ‘on fēonda geweald’ is ‘into the foes’ power’, ‘fēonda’ a genitive plural and ‘geweald’ ‘power’, and ‘forð’ is ‘forth’. ‘snūde forsended’ is ‘swiftly sent away’, a participle of ‘forsendan’. ‘mid Ēotenum’ is ‘among the Eotens’. Klaeber capitalises the word for a people, probably the Jutes, though a few editors write ‘eotenum’ with a small letter for the giants, as at 883 (the apparatus lists Kemble, Holthausen, Chambers); either way they are enemies.

sentences.t:
Hine sorhwylmas
lemede tō lange;
sentences.l: Him sorrow-surges lamed too long;
sentences.i: Surges of sorrow crippled him for too long;
sentences.n: ‘Hine’ is accusative and ‘sorhwylmas’ the nominative plural subject: ‘sorh’, ‘sorrow’, and ‘wylm’, ‘welling, surge’, so waves of grief or care. ‘lemede’ is the past of ‘lemian’, ‘lame, cripple’, here ‘crush’; it is singular where the subject is plural, and the apparatus lists editors who write ‘lemedon’ (Grundtvig, Kemble, Holthausen) or read ‘sorhwylma hrine’ (Bugge), ‘touch of sorrow-surges’, so the form is a doubt. ‘tō lange’ is ‘too long’. The cause of the sorrow is not given in these lines.

sentences.t:
hē his lēodum wearð,
eallum æþellingum tō aldorceare;
sentences.l: he to his people became, to all athelings, to a life-care;
sentences.i: he became a lasting sorrow to his people, to all the athelings;
sentences.n: ‘hē’ is still Heremōd, and ‘wearð’ is ‘became’ again. ‘his lēodum’ is ‘to his people’, dative plural, and ‘eallum æþellingum’ is ‘to all the athelings’, in apposition. ‘tō aldorceare’ is ‘to a life-care’: ‘aldor’ is ‘life’ (as in ‘aldorgedāl’, ‘life-parting’, in the twelfth part) and ‘cearu’ ‘sorrow’, so a sorrow that lasts a lifetime, or a deadly sorrow; the ending is a dative. He proved a grief to his own people, not a help.

sentences.t:
swylce oft bemearn ǣrran mǣlum
swīðferhþes sīð snotor ceorl monig,
sentences.l: likewise often lamented at earlier times the strong-minded one’s journey a wise man, many a one,
sentences.i: Likewise, many a wise man in former times often grieved over the course of that stern-minded one,
sentences.n: ‘swylce’ is ‘likewise’. ‘bemearn’ is the past of ‘bemurnan’, ‘mourn over’, with an accusative object, ‘sīð’, ‘journey’, ‘course’, here his way of going on or his departure. ‘ǣrran mǣlum’ is ‘at earlier times’, a dative plural, ‘ǣrra’ being ‘former’ and ‘mǣl’ ‘time’. ‘swīðferhþes’ is the genitive of ‘swīðferhþ’, ‘strong-minded’, here ‘stern, stubborn’: ‘swīð’, ‘strong’, and ‘ferhþ’, ‘spirit’, its first part the same as in ‘swīðhicgende’ at 919. ‘snotor ceorl monig’ is ‘wise man, many a one’, with ‘ceorl’, a free man (the ancestor of ‘churl’), and ‘snotor’ in the nominative. The mourners are the wise among the Danes.

sentences.t:
sē þe him bealwa tō bōte gelȳfde,
þæt þæt ðēodnes bearn geþēon scolde,
fæderæþelum onfōn, folc gehealdan,
hord ond hlēoburh, hæleþa rīce,
ēþel Scyldinga.
sentences.l: who in him for a remedy of evils trusted, that the prince’s child should thrive, receive the father-nobility, hold the folk, the hoard and shelter-burg, the heroes’ kingdom, the homeland of Scyldings.
sentences.i: the man who trusted in him as a remedy for evils, believing that the prince’s son would thrive, would take up his father’s rank, keep the people, the hoard and the sheltering stronghold, the realm of heroes, the home of the Scyldings.
sentences.n: ‘sē þe’ is ‘he who’, and ‘him … gelȳfde’ is ‘trusted in him’, the thing trusted being ‘tō bōte bealwa’, ‘for a remedy of evils’ (‘bealwa’ the genitive plural of ‘bealu’, ‘evil’; ‘bōt’ is ‘remedy’). The clause after ‘þæt þæt’ says what the trust was: ‘ðēodnes bearn’ is ‘the prince’s child’, who should ‘geþēon’, ‘thrive’, ‘onfōn’, ‘receive’, ‘fæderæþelum’, which I take as a dative plural of ‘fæderæþelu’, ‘father’s noble rank’ (Thorkelin and others write it as two words), and ‘gehealdan’, ‘hold’, ‘folc’, ‘hord ond hlēoburh’, ‘hoard and shelter-burg’, with ‘hlēo’ ‘shelter’ and ‘burh’ ‘stronghold’. ‘hæleþa rīce’ is ‘the heroes’ kingdom’ and ‘ēþel Scyldinga’ ‘the homeland of the Scyldings’, the Danes’ own name for themselves. At 913 the manuscript has only three marks, a dot, the rune ᛟ and a dot; the rune is called ‘ēðel’, ‘homeland’, and a scribe who wrote a rune for its name would have it read as the word, so I take the word as ‘ēþel’; that is a reading from the rune’s name, not a certainty. The wise men hoped Heremōd would inherit the Danes’ kingdom.

sentences.l: He there to all became, Higelac’s kinsman, to the kin of men, to friends more pleasing;
sentences.i: There Higelac’s kinsman became dear to all, to the race of men, more pleasing to his friends;
sentences.n: ‘Hē’ now is Beowulf, ‘mǣg Higelāces’, ‘Higelac’s kinsman’, in apposition; ‘wearð’ repeats the verb of 905 on purpose, so that the two are set side by side: one became a sorrow, the other became dear. ‘eallum … manna cynne’ is ‘to all, to the race of men’. ‘frēondum gefægra’ is ‘more pleasing to friends’, ‘gefægra’ being a comparative. The word is uncertain: ‘gefæge’ (short æ, not the ‘fǣge’ of 846) is ‘glad, pleasing’, but the apparatus lists Kemble’s ‘gef[r]ǣgra’, ‘better known, more famous’, and Grundtvig’s ‘gefægenra’, ‘gladder’. I give ‘more pleasing’, a guess. ‘þǣr’ is ‘there’, in that case.

sentences.t: hine fyren onwōd.
sentences.l: him crime invaded.
sentences.i: wickedness took hold of him.
sentences.n: ‘hine’ is Heremōd again, the object. ‘fyren’ is the nominative, ‘crime, sin’, as in ‘fyrena’ at 879, and ‘onwōd’ is the past of ‘onwadan’, ‘wade into, invade, seize’. The two men are set against each other: one became dear to everyone, the other was overrun by crime. The poet does not say here what the crime was.

sentences.t:
Hwīlum flītende fealwe strǣte
mēarum mǣton.
sentences.l: At whiles contending, they fallow roads with horses measured.
sentences.i: Sometimes, racing one another, they measured the dun roads with their horses.
sentences.n: ‘Hwīlum’ is ‘at whiles’ again, and the riders of 864 are back. ‘flītende’ is a present participle, nominative plural, from ‘flītan’, ‘strive, contend’ (cf. ‘flite’), so racing. ‘fealwe strǣte’ is ‘fallow roads’, accusative plural, the same word ‘fealwe’ (‘pale brown, dun’) that was given to the horses at 865; ‘strǣt’ is the Latin ‘strata’, a paved road. ‘mēarum’ is a dative plural, ‘with horses’, and ‘mǣton’ is a guess: the past plural of ‘metan’, ‘measure’, here ‘cover’, to measure a road by riding it. I know of no other sense of the verb that fits, so I keep ‘measured’, but it remains a guess. The apparatus lists ‘fealwum’ (Aantekeningen), ‘with dun’.

sentences.t:
Ðā wæs morgenlēoht
scofen ond scynded.
sentences.l: Then was the morning-light shoved forward and hurried.
sentences.i: Then the morning light was driven on and hurried along.
sentences.n: ‘Ðā’ is ‘then’. ‘morgenlēoht’ is ‘morning-light’, the subject. ‘scofen ond scynded’ are two participles after ‘wæs’: ‘scofen’ is from ‘scūfan’, ‘shove’, and ‘scynded’ from ‘scyndan’, ‘hasten’, so pushed on and hurried. The sense is that the morning wore on while they rode and listened, so the time has come for the king to appear.

sentences.l: Went many a retainer, strong-minded, to the hall, the high, the cunning-wonder to see;
sentences.i: Many a retainer went, stout-hearted, to the high hall to see the marvel;
sentences.n: ‘Ēode’ is the past singular of ‘gān’, ‘go’, with a collective subject, ‘scealc monig’, ‘many a retainer’. ‘swīðhicgende’ is ‘swīð’, ‘strong’, and ‘hicgende’, ‘thinking’, so ‘strong-minded, resolute’, like ‘heardhicgende’ in the twelfth part. ‘tō sele þām hēan’ is ‘to the hall, the high’, with ‘hēan’ the weak dative; ‘sele’ is the hall. ‘searowundor’ is ‘searu’, ‘skill, device’, and ‘wundor’, ‘wonder’, so a wonder made by skill; the compound is rare and the exact sense is a guess. The thing is not named in these lines; the infinitive ‘sēon’ is the aim, ‘to see’.

sentences.t:
swylce self cyning
of brȳdbūre, bēahhorda weard,
tryddode tīrfæst getrume micle,
sentences.l: likewise the king himself from the bride-bower, the ring-hoards’ guardian, trod, glory-fast, with a company great,
sentences.i: And the king himself came from the women’s chamber, the keeper of the ring-hoards, striding in firm glory with a great company,
sentences.n: ‘swylce’ is ‘likewise’. ‘self cyning’ is ‘the king himself’, nominative, and the king is Hrōðgār, named at 863. ‘of brȳdbūre’ is ‘from the bride-bower’, ‘brȳd’, ‘bride, woman’, and ‘būr’, ‘chamber’, the women’s quarters. ‘bēahhorda weard’ is ‘keeper of the ring-hoards’, ‘weard’ being a guard and ‘bēahhorda’ a genitive plural. ‘tryddode’ is the past of the weak verb ‘tryddian’, ‘tread, step’ (related to ‘treddan’), and ‘tīrfæst’ is ‘tīr’, ‘glory’, and ‘fæst’, ‘firm’, so firm in glory, as the word ‘steadfast’ is made. ‘getrume micle’ is ‘with a great troop’, a dative: ‘getrum’ means a body of men.

sentences.t:
cystum gecȳþed, ond his cwēn mid him
medostigge mæt mægþa hōse.
sentences.l: by virtues made known, and his queen with him the mead-path measured, with a troop of maidens.
sentences.i: known for his many virtues, and his queen with him walked the way to the mead-hall, with a company of ladies.
sentences.n: ‘cystum gecȳþed’ is ‘by excellences made known’, ‘gecȳþed’ the participle of ‘gecȳþan’, ‘make known’, so famous for his noble qualities; ‘cystum’ is the same word as at 867. ‘ond his cwēn mid him’ is ‘and his queen with him’, the queen having no name here. ‘medostigge’ is ‘medu’, ‘mead’, and ‘stig’, ‘path’, the way she trod and the object of ‘mæt’, so I take it as an accusative, though its ending would also fit a dative (‘along the mead-path’), and ‘mæt’ is the past singular of ‘metan’, ‘measure’, here ‘walked the length of’, as at 917. ‘mægþa hōse’ is ‘a troop of maidens’: ‘hōs’ is ‘band, company’, and ‘mægþa’ is the genitive plural of ‘mægþ’, which can be ‘maiden’ or ‘family’; I take ‘maidens’ because the women’s party fits, but the choice is a guess. The fitt ends as the king comes into the hall.
